draft.title: Solving equations with graphs
card: To solve f(x) = g(x), draw y = f(x) and y = g(x) on the same axes. At a point where the graphs meet, both functions give the same y value for that x.
The solutions are the x values of the intersection points. The y values are not the solutions.
The number of intersection points is the number of solutions. Two crossing points mean two solutions, one touching point means one, and no meeting means none.
Example: y = x² and y = 4 meet at (−2, 4) and (2, 4). So x² = 4 has two solutions, x = −2 and x = 2.
draft.remember: Solutions of f(x) = g(x) are the x values where the graphs meet, one for each meeting point.

a.q: The graphs of y = f(x) and y = g(x) meet at (1, 5) and (3, 5). What are the solutions of f(x) = g(x)?
opts: x = 1 and x = 3
x = 1, x = 3 and x = 5
x = 5 only, found twice
a.why: Solutions are the x values of the meeting points, which are 1 and 3. The y value 5 is tempting, but it is the common height of the graphs, not a solution for x.
a.clue: Which coordinate of each meeting point is the solution?

b.q: The line y = 2 and the parabola y = x² + 3 are drawn on the same axes. The parabola never goes below y = 3. How many solutions does x² + 3 = 2 have?
opts: None, because the graphs never meet
One, because the line is horizontal
Two, because a parabola is a quadratic
Three, because there are three terms
b.why: The parabola's lowest point is y = 3, which is above the line y = 2, so the graphs never meet. No intersections means no solutions. A quadratic does not always have two solutions, as the graphs may not meet.
b.clue: Compare the height of the line with the lowest point of the parabola.

b.best: None, because the graphs never meet

final.title: Solving equations with graphs
card: To solve \(f(x) = g(x)\), draw \(y = f(x)\) and \(y = g(x)\) on the same axes. At a point where the graphs meet, both functions give the same \(y\) value for that \(x\).
The solutions are the \(x\) values of the intersection points. The \(y\) values are not the solutions.
The number of intersection points is the number of solutions. Two crossing points mean two solutions, one touching point means one, and no meeting means none.
Example: \(y = x^{2}\) and \(y = 4\) meet at \((-2, 4)\) and \((2, 4)\). So \(x^{2} = 4\) has two solutions, \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\).

4.alt: The parabola \(y = x^{2}\) and the line \(y = 4\). They meet at \((-2, 4)\) and \((2, 4)\). Dashed lines down to the x-axis show the solutions of \(x^{2} = 4\): \(x = -2\) and \(x = 2\).

final.remember: Solutions of \(f(x) = g(x)\) are the \(x\) values where the graphs meet, one for each meeting point.

a.q: The graphs of \(y = f(x)\) and \(y = g(x)\) meet at \((1, 5)\) and \((3, 5)\). What are the solutions of \(f(x) = g(x)\)?
opts: \(x = 5\) only, found twice
a.why: Solutions are the \(x\) values of the meeting points, which are 1 and 3. The \(y\) value 5 is tempting, but it is the common height of the graphs, not a solution for \(x\).
a.clue: Which coordinate of each meeting point is the solution?

b.q: The line \(y = 2\) and the parabola \(y = x^{2} + 3\) are drawn on the same axes. The parabola never goes below \(y = 3\). How many solutions does \(x^{2} + 3 = 2\) have?
opts: None, because the graphs never meet
One, because the line is horizontal
Two, because a parabola is a quadratic
Three, because there are three terms
b.why: The parabola's lowest point is \(y = 3\), which is above the line \(y = 2\), so the graphs never meet. No intersections means no solutions. A quadratic does not always have two solutions, as the graphs may not meet.
b.clue: Compare the height of the line with the lowest point of the parabola.
